subtopic: CANADIAN CENTRE FOR MANAGEMENT DEVELOPMENT ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a privilege to rise to speak to Bill C-34, an act to establish the Canadian Centre for Management Development.
This centre has four specific objectives: developing the knowledge and skills of managers, developing the service ethic, originate research into practical solutions to the problems faced by public administrators, and advancing the commitment to public sector management excellence. These are worth-while objectives and, as such, we in the New Democratic Party are proud to support this bill.
At the outset I would like to say that this centre is an idea whose time has come and that, in the proper context, it can help those who run the Public Service deal with the fast pace of change in today's world. It will help them cope with fast-breaking issues and new technologies. It will serve to keep the Public Service on the cutting edge of change rather than following in its wake trying to catch up.
The Canadian Centre for Management Development is a response to a world-wide change in management practices. Today's managers must be able to question the status quo. Where once unthinking obedience to hierarchy was required of managers, today they must be able to think, to analyse and to conceptualize. Today's managers must focus on people rather than bureaucracy. These are changes that I applaud.
I worry that this centre is also a response to other less beneficial changes in our country; namely, the effects of six years of the Tory agenda.
Mr. Jack Manion, the principal of the centre, has often linked the centre to the government's right-wing agenda for the Public Service. In his words, that agenda is to "decentralize, deregulate, deburden and debureaucra-tize". This means that the centre will be geared to

May 18, 1990
Government Orders
getting its managers to squeeze out more performance with fewer people and less money.
On a similar note, the centre is frequently connected with Public Service 2000, a shadowy effort also intended to strengthen the hand of upper management under the mantra of letting managers manage, even at the expense of collective bargaining rights.
Given the centre's $11.5 million budget, money obviously is not a problem for upper management. One-third of the permanent staff earn of average of $86,000 a year and the centre is not required to recover costs through tuition fees. That this occurs at a time of fiscal restraint illustrates one of the key problems with the Public Service. Top-level managers invariably choose to make cuts at the bottom of the totem-pole, leaving the fat at the top intact. The totem-pole is tottering. It is top-heavy with managers who have been securing their own jobs while cutting those underneath them. Those managers have been increasing their own salaries while letting salaries in general fall behind the cost of living. If the government is committed to reducing bureaucracy, it should start at the top and work down, rather than cutting the services that directly affect the lives of Canadians everywhere.
I share the concern that this centre is to some extent a reflection of that philosophy, and that it will further isolate mandarins in an ivory tower of their own, safe from the storm clouds emerging as a result of the cutbacks they are being trained to administer. Unless those workers on the front lines have a say in how the Public Service is managed, then no amount of academia will serve. It is the customs officials, the NRC scientists and CEIC receptionists who know what Canadians want and expect from the Public Service, and their voices should echo through the halls of power.
I would caution the government that our support for C-34 is not an endorsement of privatization, contracting out, and downsizing-activities that have cut close to 10,000 jobs from the Public Service in the last five years. No amount of managerial training can heal the wounds this has caused. There is widespread demoralization throughout the Public Service caused by stalled careers and staffs cut to the bone. Pretending that poor performance is a management problem rather than a budget
problem is a little like not giving a sea captain a rudder, but all the training needed to go down with the ship.
The real problem is not management, but the ability of the government to hack and slash without regard to the effects on the Public Service to carry out the important roles expected of it, including the protection of health and safety of the average person. The Treasury Board, the Privy Council, and the Public Service Commission control 10 per cent of national expenditures and a workforce of a quarter of a million. Yet, no committee of the House routinely studies the cumulative social costs of all of this budget cutting.
I worry that this centre will accelerate this tendency to see costs-benefits analysis in purely economic rather than social terms. Mr. Manion, for example, has been actively soliciting the influence of corporations, putting the CEOs and chairmen of major corporations on the centre's board of governors. Will the up-and-coming managers of tomorrow be required to think of government as just another bottom-line business, rather than as the defender of those who have fallen through the cracks of our profit-oriented society? This is especially critical in that Mr. Manion envisions his centre as an influential voice in the shaping of over-all government policy and procedures.
When reports such as Beneath the Veneer reveal the extent of the obstacles faced by women in the Public Service, it is important that such an influential centre be more than just a training school for Ottawa's mandarins. We cannot allow the centre to become another old boys' network, perpetuating the same elites from the same families, from the same parts of the country. Those same people all too often end up at the top. Room must be made for those who have traditionally been frozen out of the power structure: visible minorities, women, aboriginal people, and the disabled.
Mr. Manion has said that "to give priority to access over good management could be detrimental to the fundamental objective of the centre, which is to produce quality management". I find statements such as that worrying, especially since the bill also aims to "foster among Public Service managers a sense of the purpose, values and traditions of the Public Service". We in the House are aware, I am sure, that these purposes, values and traditions are largely white and male, set in a context dominated by white men. I am sure that Mr. Manion would agree that talent knows no racial or gender
May 18, 1990

boundaries and we can have fair participation of all minority groups without jeopardizing quality.
When only 12 per cent of senior management is female, 0.8 per cent aboriginal, 1.5 per cent disabled and 1.8 per cent members of visible minorities, one can only wonder how many talented people are out there whose skills could be helping to build this country, but whose talents are instead untapped because of the blindness of our prejudices.
We hope that the centre will serve to change the attitudes of the influential decision-makers it trains. This can be done by exposing what is essentially a homogeneous population to people of differing races and cultures. It will be only by working alongside the disabled, women, aboriginals, and visible minorities, that we can overcome our biases toward them. I hope the centre will make good on its promises to include target groups on its board, in its classrooms, and teaching at its podiums.
We in the NDP are happy to see that the centre has taken steps to provide this kind of access and, that it is willing to be a vehicle through which we can sensitize managers to the country's tremendous racial and cultural diversity, as well as to the sorts of unconscious prejudices we all have. Unless the people at the top understand the needs of those who have been kept at the bottom, we can never have a society in which anyone with talent and skill can make her or his mark in the world.

subtopic: CANADIAN CENTRE FOR MANAGEMENT DEVELOPMENT ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to join in the debate today on third reading of Bill 0-34, an act to establish the Canadian Centre for Management Development.
I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier who first raised this idea in 1974. I am sure he will share our pleasure that the government has reintroduced this bill. It is a tribute to my colleague and members on this side of the House that the government has adopted this Liberal initiative. I would like to congratulate the government on introducing this bill.
This bill is before us again because there is a very real need for a centre for management development in the country. The world today is an increasingly competitive
Government Orders
place. Success, in a lot of ways, depends upon the ability of a nation to manage its internal and external activities and resources with efficiency and creativity.
The centre, of course, will provide that ideal forum for fostering awareness and advocating excellence within the Public Service. It can also set an example for its counterpart in the private sector to follow.
Canada's Public Service is currently facing many challenges with difficulties in areas such as downsizing. We have close to about 13,000 employees and their families who have been affected since 1985. Any hiring done today is for term positions with less security and fewer benefits for the employee.
Another problem is the issue of aging. The average age of public servants is increasing, with the majority in the 30 to 54 years age bracket.
Yet another problem is plateauing. There are fewer opportunities for career advancement due to cut-backs and the large number of public servants with seniority.
But more than anything else, there is a major problem within the Public Service with respect to equal opportunity. My colleague from Ottawa West has put forward some resolutions to the House on the question of equal opportunity. I was informed that these recommendations were not adopted. It is quite unfortunate they were not.
Women are still mainly at a disadvantage, especially when we talk about administrative support positions. Women make up 83 per cent of the employees at this level, but they also hold 60 per cent of the term positions within the Public Service. Women are under-represented in every other occupation within the Public Service.
Perhaps most seriously, while women represent more than 42 per cent of the Public Service workforce, they represent only 12.3 per cent at the management level.
While visible minority groups also make up almost 5 per cent of the Canadian labour force, they represent only 1.7 per cent of the Public Service.
Workers who are disabled make up 6 per cent of the national labour force, but represent only 1.9 of the Public Service.

May 18, 1990
Government Orders
I was informed that, to date, attempts to achieve employment equity have not been veiy successful. Aboriginal peoples, disabled persons, members of visible minority groups, and women are still under-represented in the Public Service.
It is little wonder that morale is a serious problem in the Public Service sector. Employees must cope with the real possibility that their jobs may not exist tomorrow, and that, even if they hang on to their job, there is very little opportunity for advancement.
These concerns can and, indeed, must be addressed by the new Canadian Centre for Management Development. The centre will provide the ideal forum for fostering awareness and advocating change within the Public Service.
When serious issues such as employment equity and efficiency need to be addressed, there is no better place to start than at the top. Obviously, a management development centre will provide a forum in which values and priorities such as equity and excellence can be promoted.
When Max Yalden, the Chairman of the Canadian Human Rights Commission, addressed the legislative committee studying this bill, he said, and I quote:
If the Canadian Centre for Management Development is to be effective in promoting excellence in the Public Service-human rights principles must be an integral part of a manager's approach to problem solving, not an add-on to be trotted out for inspection on appropriate occasions.
I could not agree more.
This centre must help put into action the values and priorities which the Employment Equity Act and the Canadian Multiculturalism Act are built on, but which to date have failed to be put into practice.
There is another serious issue that the Centre for Management Development must address. In this time of fiscal restraint and increasing competition, the Public Service, like those in the private sector, must focus on maximum productivity and effective use of resources, both human and financial.
Government initiatives such as downsizing, combined with very real changes in the national and international arena, have resulted in a greater need than ever before for organizational and operational excellence within our Public Service.
Managers must address the serious dilemmas facing their employees. Better communication and understanding between all levels within the Public Service will enable the various departments to function more smoothly and, obviously, more effectively.
The days are long gone when this country could afford to waste human resources. Canada is well known for its natural resources, but let me suggest that it is our people which are the most valuable of all our assets.
Yet, lack of motivation and low morale can affect the efficiency and quality of work of those employed in the Public Service. The problems of restraint, and the bleak prospects for advancement could be steering good people away from the Public Service.
The Centre for Management Development is the place to start if we are going to address this very real and serious problem. The public policy demands of the future will require intelligent and creative solutions. It is up to us today to ensure that we have prepared our public service for the challenges ahead.
It is my hope that the problems currently facing the Public Service and the increasingly urgent need for efficient and productive management skills will be addressed by the creation of this Canadian Centre for Management Development.
I am certain we will all agree that Canada has an excellent Public Service, perhaps one of the finest in the world, made up of employees committed to maintaining a high level of competency and excellence in the service area. However, we cannot take our public servants for granted.
The steps we take today will determine the quality and nature of our Public Service of tomorrow. The establishment of the centre will ensure that Canada heads into the 21st century with a highly skilled and adaptable Public Service at the helm.
Madam Speaker, I would like to thank you for this opportunity to speak on this bill, and once again I would like to thank my colleagues from Ottawa-Vanier and Ottawa West for helping to make this discussion a productive one.

Madam Speaker, I am honoured to speak at third reading of Bill C-57.
As hon. members know, this bill gives a unique type of intellectual property protection for designers of microchip topographies. It is a reflection of the new and modern society that we live in where these microchips play an ever-increasing role in all the manufacturing equipment and tools that we use daily.
Madam Speaker, you will know that the bill was introduced on December 18, 1989. It was debated at second reading and referred to a legislative committee on March 9. The legislative committee was struck on March 14, witnesses were heard and the committee reported back to this House, with amendments, on April 11, 1990. Those amendments reflect the evidence that the committee heard, and the good work performed by the members of that committee.
There was broad public support from the Patent and Trademark Institute of Canada, the Information Technology Association of Canada as well as the Canadian Bar Association. In this country, we have some 25 Canadian firms that design these types of microchips.
I would like to extend thanks on behalf of the committee to the officials; Mr. David Watters as Director General, Johanne Daniel, the Policy Analyst and Allan Troicuk, the Senior Legal Analyst. These officials were vital to us, because most of the members do not appreciate yet the significance of this new technology. Indeed, we hardly know the vocabulary. They were most helpful to us.
I would also like to extend thanks to the legislative chairman, the distinguished member for Welland-St. Catharines-Thorold, and members of the committee, such as the hon. member for Carleton-Gloucester who

In short, this is good public policy for the country for the future. Parliament has acted well in a matter of four or five months. I think it speaks well for the future and how this Parliament should act on bills that are good public policy.

Your kindness is unsurpassed, Madam Speaker!

The Liberal party is pleased to support Bill C-57. The hon. member for Lethbridge made a wonderful presentation today and did an excellent job at the legislative committee level. I commend him. I found him to be very attentive and co-operative most of the time.
I have to admit that he is a good listener. Whether he reacts positively to everyone's request is another subject.

As far as integrated circuits go, for some time now we have been noticing that if we examine the innards of our refrigerators, our washing machines, our dishwashers, our cars and every electronic device we find, that they all have integrated circuits. We are now into the 90s and we are bound to see ever more industrial and electronic circuitry development. Most of these products come
from the United States. In Canada we have about 25 firms which specialize in this field. I believe that close to $1 billion is spent on such circuits. Canadian and foreign companies involved in the design and production of integrated circuits need some kind of protection. It would be a shame if our country failed to protect designers and inventors in these various fields.
This is such a new field of endeavour that it may have been neglected over the past five years. I was told that the government has spent at least that much time getting ready to introduce this legislation. Well, now we have it, and the Liberals agree that we need this kind of measure. I sat on the legislative committee and I am aware that it raises a few problems, in the sense that we need a statute which will command respect on the part of the Americans if only because they happen to be our major trade partners. I know that five or six years ago the United States did legislate to protect the designers and owners of integrated circuits.
We all know that Europe 92 will soon be reality and that Europeans are involved in integrated circuitry development. This is true as well of such Far East countries as Japan, Taiwan, and Korea. All nations should get together on some kind of international agreement. As I understand it, the legislative committee studied a proposition for an international agreement according to which, countries would respect each others legislation concerning integrated circuits. That is necessary. Unfortunately, there is a disagreement between the Americans and the proponents of an international legislation or agreement.
Our measure seems based on the American law. I can live with that since the Americans are our main trading partners. But, while listening to the speeches in legislative committee, I could not help but ask myself questions about the American law since we often confuse the American and Canadian ways of doing things because we watch so much American television.

This is not Canadian law. Many times Canadians watching TV take for granted that this is the way law in North America is established. We know well that our laws are different in Canada. Originally they came from Great Britain.
May 18, 1990



And we also have the Napoleonic Code.

There are laws that are pertinent to the country; they are federal laws. There are laws that are pertinent to the provinces, and each province has a set of laws. We see this in property legislation, for example. If you want to purchase some land or a house, the laws that are applicable are those of the provinces.
That interests me a great deal. I did appreciate the discussions and dialogue that we had. Five or six members from the integrated circuit community explained to us what a topography of a circuit was. They gave a very interesting explanation of integrated circuit topography. They drew a cross-section of a cityscape where you could see many buildings of different sizes and different heights. If you slice it in two, as a jolly giant would, you get an idea what it would look like from the other extremity, the viewpoint of a small bug. You could see what a chip looks like from a side view.
That was really interesting and we all learned a great deal. We even all learned to pronounce the words correctly. It was quite an enjoyable and educational activity.
As a former high school teacher and school administrator, and being on this legislative committee for the very first time as a new member of Parliament, I became more and more curious about science and technology. I asked that certain witnesses appear before us. I appreciated the committee accepting a witness from the National Research Council of Canada.
We did have a presentation from the in-house lawyer-scientist from the National Research Council. At the very least, he was most provocative. He certainly made the member for Lethbridge listen veiy attentively on quite a few occasions, as he did all of us.
He was obviously challenged because he was not flowing in the same vein as the government side. He did not have the chance to prepare at length. The NRC did not have a chance to verify thoroughly his presentation, so his presentation was really one of an in-house
Government Orders
lawyer-scientist house who made a personal presentation with the authority of the NRC authorities. However, they did not have time, or did not want to take the time, to verify his presentation.
I find it deplorable that the president of the NRC wrote a letter to the committee chairman stating that this gentleman was not representing the NRC's official position. He was a witness called by Parliament to give his impressions. He was not someone we picked off the street. He was someone accorded permission to come and speak to us.
On the final day of the hearings I presented a request to have another witness come in. I had my assistant call every faculty of law in Canada to find out who would be willing to give an opinion on this presentation by the person from the NRC. We found two such persons. One was David Vaver, Professor of Law from the most reputable institution, Osgoode Law School. This is his particular domain.
He wrote to me at great length. I did present the letter to the committee chairman and I gave copies to all the members of the committee. I was astounded that my request to hear this gentleman, who is a national expert in constitutional law and in this field that we are discussing today, was turned down.
This is no reflection on the member for Lethbridge who was present at all times and made terrific contributions. The staff from the Consumer and Corporate Affairs ministry made a beautiful presentation. They were very erudite and explained at length everything that they were doing. I commend them for their work. I commend them for their presentation. I commend them for the proposed law. However, I was dismayed that when I proposed that this final witness come in, all of a sudden a whole group of Conservative members came in and sat down, some of whom could not even pronounce half of the words in the text, and decided that no more witnesses would appear. I was quite displeased with this.
Therefore, knowing that I have all the time I need to make a response to the member for Lethbridge, I would like to have inserted in the record that there was a report presented to the legislative committee on this bill by Mr. Alan T. Blackwell, the intellectual property advisor of the National Research Council of Canada. He is both a lawyer and a scientist.

May 18, 1990
Government Orders
I would like to submit to the House the letter in response-and I believe it would be called an opinion- from Professor David Vaver of the University of York, Osgoode Hall Law School.
The ministry did deal with the opinion from Professor David Vaver and made a response that was sent through the mail to different members. Of course, in my mind, it was oriented to the government's view. My experience in municipal politics is that whenever you bring in experts, whether engineers or contractors, or experts in public accounts, accounting or law, if you bring in two of them to make a presentation, you will have contradicting views. If you bring in five of them, you could possibly have five contradicting views. The trick is to choose the one that is going to be closest to your philosophy or to the response you would like to hear.
Perhaps that is the reason why the courts are overly busy. That is perhaps the reason we see so many wealthy lawyers today and law firms with as many as 400 or 500 members. That is in Canada. I understand that in the United States there are firms with thousands of members.
I can well understand and I can appreciate the work of judges, especially since I spent the whole evening and all night, with just a couple of hours of sleep, comparing the text of the NRC lawyer with the text of the opinion of the professor from Osgoode Law School and the response from the Ministry of Justice to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
I will attempt to give an of overview of what they said because I really think this should be on the books.
The creators should be protected. They need to be protected, and this party is going to support this law. These people are going to be protected for 10 years. Also, this law is going to be on the books for at least five years. At the end of five years the minister will be able to call for a review, which could take another year. That is six years. It could well be another 10 years before we see any revision of this law. I find that extremely unfortunate. I find it unfortunate that after dragging its feet for five years now, all of a sudden the government wants to pass this law within hours.
I am also aware that the American government has been supporting the Canadian creators, inventors and owners of these integrated circuits for six-month periods. It has been repeating that for two or three years. Our six-month period is coming up, possibly at the end of the year, and that could have been renewed again. So the urgency of it makes me wonder why we are so much in a hurry.
I would like to quote from the reports I have read and the material I have gathered together. I would like to quote Alan T. Blackwell, the gentleman from the NRC. He begins by raising a constitutional question. He says:
Bill C-57 attempts to deal partly with the problem of ownership in s.7, but it exceeds Parliament's constitutional power. s.7(l) says:
"A topography, whether registered or unregistered, is
transferable, either as to the whole interest therein or to any
undivided portion thereof."
The first problem is logical: s.7 says that the topography is transferable, but what is important is that certain rights concerning a topography be transferable. The topography is just a design, and is obviously transferable.
The second problem is conceptual: s.7 assumes the very doubtful underlying idea that some kind of ownership of the design exists in the first place. Saying something is transferable does not say what it is, and does not necessarily prove that it exists.
The third problem is constitutional: even if there is some kind of ownership of a design, it is probably not within the power of the federal government to legislate with respect to that ownership. The federal government cannot create common law, nor new species of property. The federal government does not have power over property and civil rights in the provinces. It has power in the area of patents and copyright, but that is because those areas are enumerated in s.91 of the Constitution Act, 1867.
Topographies are not part of the law of patents. They could be part of the law of copyright, but that is explicitly excluded by this Bill.
s.7 might be constitutionally acceptable if it said that the rights granted by the Act are transferable. That is different from saying that topographies, including unregistered ones, are transferable.
s.7 might also be constitutionally justified if the topographies affected were involved in interprovincial commerce. However, as written, s.7 would apply with equal force to commerce entirely within a province. It also applies to topographies not seeking the benefit of the Bill, and to topographies not in in any way involving the federal Crown. One could argue that in the normal course of events topographies move interprovincially, but basing legislation on such a shaky argument is unwise, especially when workable alternatives exist.
Professor Vaver from Osgoode Hall states:
May 18, 1990

Government Orders
Mr. Blackwell raises the fundamental question of Parliament's competence to enact Bill C-57. In his view, Bill C-57 cannot rest on Parliament's power over "patents of invention and discovery", and reliance on Parliament's power to regulate trade and commerce would be unduly constrictive.
He is referring there to pages 8 and 9 of Mr. Blackwell's brief. Professor Vaver goes on to state:
I agree with Mr. Blackwell that Parliament cannot say who owns the actual chip that includes a topography, any more than it can say that 1 don't own the book I buy from a bookstore. This is a question of provincial law. But, if Parliament can create a copyright in a topography, it can create in respect of topography rights that can exist with or without registration. It has done precisely that in the Copyright Act, including in 1988 for computer programs.
Although Mr. Blackwell draws some inapposite conclusions from cl. 33(1), I agree with him that the drafting of the subsection can be improved. I think the major difficulty stems from the fact that the definitions of "design" differ under the Copyright Act and under Bill C-57.
I do not like Mr. Blackwell's suggestion (Brief, p.9) to change clause 33(1) to read: "Copyright shall not subsist in any topography." That indeed would undermine the copyright foundation for Bill C-57! I prefer his wording at the bottom of the page, with the underlined addition:
"This Act does not apply to topographies capable of being registered under the Integrated Circuit Topography Act, and shall be deemed never to have applied to topographies that, had the Integrated Circuit Topography Act been in force when the topography was created, would have then been capable of being so registered."
This is a little wordy, I admit. It has the advantage of using language already in the Copyright Act (as Mr. Blackwell points out). Moreover, that language has already been definitively interpreted: Bayliner Marine Corp. v. Doral Boats Ltd. (1986) 9 C.I.P.R. 311 (Fed. C.A.), followed in Interlego A.G. v. Tyco Industries Inc. (1988)-My underlined addition resolves, as Mr. Blackwell's language does not, the status of pre-Bill C-57 topographies: they never gained protection under the Copyright Act.
Mr. Vaver continues:
Mr. Blackwell says a design is "nothing more than information" (Brief, p 3). This is strictly true. It flows from the definition of topography in cl. 2(1): "design, however expressed". This suggests that a design need not be expressed in some fixed form but can be conveyed orally, although I don't think the Bill would be interpreted to mean that "expressed" includes merely "expressed in the creator's mind". A court would probably interpret "however expressed" as meaning "however expressed in some material form". Perhaps the definition could be usefully amended by including these clarifying words.
Mr. Vaver's fourth point is:
Mr. Blackwell finds the issue of ownership of a topography confusing-So do I (although his reading is largely coloured by his, I believe wrong, views on the constitutional issue, which lead to his view that Bill C-57 does not create a "copyright" in topography but instead depends on the civil law relating to ownership of ideas). For example, rights are granted only in respect of a registered topography and yet the Bill grants "the creator" the right to register; but nowhere is the "creator" made the "owner" of the design. (Brief, p.7)
The important point is that whoever authors the design should be able to convey the right to register it, by assignment, licence or contract. This requires careful drafting because, under comparable provisions in the Industrial Design Act, only the author of a design or someone (such as an employer) for whom the author has made the design for good consideration can register an industrial design. A design right, or a right to register a design, cannot be assigned. Only the design, once registered, can be assigned or licensed: Melnor Mfg. Ltd. Limited v Lido Industrial Products Ltd. (1970)-This situation must be avoided in Bill C-57, and clarifying the concept of ownership will help.
My diagnosis of the problem and its solution, however, differs from Mr. Blackwell's. In my view, the difficulty arises because the Bill defines "creator" in a quite inapposite manner. It confuses the person who actually makes the design with the person who owns (or should own) it. The two concepts are fundamentally separate and it is their intermingling that is the source of the whole later confusion.
I notice that the drafters of the detailed comments to Bill C-57, "Summary and Highlights" dated February 8, 1990, seem to be similarly confused on p. 18 of that document when they claim to have borrowed "the legal fiction of deemed creatorship-from the Copyright Act". The Copyright Act has no such deemed fiction at all. By s. 14(1) of that Act, the "author" is the "first owner of copyright", and by s. 14(3), a person with whom an "author" is employed is "the first owner of the copyright". In all Canadian intellectual property legislation hitherto, a clear distinction is made between the individual who does the intellectual work and the person, which may be his/her corporate employer or (in the Industrial Design Act) a commissioning entity who owns the right in the copyright, patent or industrial design. The Patent Act does not deem the employer of an inventor itself to be an inventor; nor does the Industrial Design Act deem the employer of the designer to be an author.
I think the other intellectual property statutes manifest a correct policy on this point and that Bill C-57 does not. They give the "flesh-and-blood" maker of an intellectual product at least the psychological satisfaction of being recognized as an inventor or author. In this, they also accord with customaiy usage and social convention. Legal ownership in the patent, design, or copyright may be in the employer; but as for recognition as the intellectual maker, to mangle an old song, "they can't take that away from me". I think it is an abuse of language to say that, if the National Research Council contracts with someone to make a topography (as Mr. Blackwell envisages on pp. 1-2 of his brief)

May 18, 1990
Government Orders
the Council should be called the topography "creator", even though it just specified the end product in terms of result but left it to the contractor how to create that result.
The Copyright Act provides an appropriate model. The drafters of Bill C-57 claim to have, but have not, followed it. Had they followed the model, then:
-the author of a topography would be the person who created it;
-he or she would be the "creator" and first owner;
-if the author was employed or commissioned, the commissioner or employer would be first owner;
-the owner of the topography would be entitled to assign his, her or its rights in the design and a simple assignment could, by the Bill, be deemed to entitle the assignee to register the topography.
The difficulty Mr. Blackwell sees about the entitlement of a Canadian importer to register a newly created Korean topography- would then be cured by adding "or owner" to cl. 4(l)(c) after the opening words "the creator".
Something like the foregoing seems to be the U.S. model, and I cannot see why Canada would want to depart from it, in a way that is moreover contrary to Canada's own intellectual property traditions. Semiconductor companies may object to their not being called "creators", but I think that, in the context of intellectual property statutes, this is a usurpation of status. The onus should be on them to show why the fundamental basis of intellectual property law should be perverted in this way, and why the model provided by the U.S. - the "creator" of this sort of protection and the country whose nationals are likely to resort most to Bill C-57 -should not be followed here. I see no difficulty that would be caused in the application to register, and I note that the Registrar is not entitled to question the information contained in an application anyway. (Bill, cl. 18(2)).
I therefore agree with the spirit of Mr. Blackwell's proposals on pages 11-13 of his brief, but not with their wordings insofar as they merely change the concept of a "creator" into a "registered creator". This is replacing one confusion with a new one.
Obviously the topic is a difficult one, and the legal aspects or the legal approach is difficult at best. It is extremely difficult to go through papers worded in legalese and to sit as a lay judge and decide who is right, who is wrong, and what exactly legislators should be doing for the Canadian companies.

We must protect Canadians. And as I was saying earlier, we have provincial laws and Canadian laws. Should our Canadian law be a mirror of what others countries do? Perhaps, if that does not contravene our laws and if that does not disturb us in our interpretations.
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, the Liberal Party supports the principle of this legislation. And today, with our vote, we will support the legislation as proposed. However, Madam Speaker, I wanted to insist on the rapidity with which the government seemed to push this legislation through the legislative committee without really listening to the Canadian experts on this matter.
I hope it is a good legislation. I hope that tomorrow, or five years down the road, we will not regret it. I hope that Canadian companies and creators, as well as owners of integrated circuits, will not have horror stories to tell and will not spend hundreds of thousands of dollars in court to defend their position on the interpretation of this legislation.

Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to rise today to speak on Bill C-57.
First, I would like to commend the committee for its work, as it was properly described by my friend from Carleton-Gloucester. It is difficult when we are challenging witnesses and trying to arrive at a perfect answer. It is not always easy but I think in this case Bill C-57 has come out of the committee with unanimous support. Protection is long overdue for Canadian manufacturers and Canadian technology and Bill C-57 endeavours to do that. Rather than prolong the passing of this bill with a lengthy debate I would terminate at this point by simply saying that the NDP unanimously supports this bill for passage at this time.
Hear, hear.
